# Initializing a Repository

After this page you have an empty Git repository on `main` and you know what `git init` created.

## A directory becomes a repository

```bash
mkdir -p ~/desk/desk-api
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git init
```

Output looks like:

```
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/ada/desk/desk-api/.git/
```

If you set `init.defaultBranch main` (chapter 2), the empty branch is named `main`. Confirm:

```bash
git status
```

```
On branch main

No commits yet

nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)
```

`~/desk/desk-api` is the **working tree**. `~/desk/desk-api/.git/` is the **repository** (objects, refs, config). You edit files next to `.git`, not inside it.

```text
~/desk/desk-api/                 working tree (you edit these)
├── README.md
├── src/
└── .git/                        repository
    ├── HEAD                     ref: refs/heads/main
    ├── config
    ├── objects/                 empty until first commit
    └── refs/heads/              main appears after first commit
```

This book’s recurring desk is three repos: `desk-web`, `desk-api`, `desk-infra`. Part I uses `desk-api` as the tiny project. Create the other two the same way when a later chapter asks.

## What `git init` wrote

```bash
ls -a .git
```

You will see at least `config`, `HEAD`, `objects/`, `refs/`. `HEAD` currently says `ref: refs/heads/main` even though `refs/heads/main` does not exist yet. The first commit creates that file.

```bash
cat .git/HEAD
git rev-parse --git-dir
# .git
```

`--git-dir` is useful when you are in a subdirectory later.

## `init` vs `clone`

| Command | When |
|---------|------|
| `git init` | You are starting a project that has no Git history yet |
| `git clone <url>` | You are copying an existing repository, including its history |

`clone` is chapter 11. For a brand-new desk project, `init` is the right verb.

## Already have files?

`git init` in a directory that already has source files is fine. Git does not add them until you `git add`. The next page is that loop.

## `init` in the wrong place

If you run `git init` in your home directory, every `git status` from a subdirectory without its own `.git` will try to use `~/.git`. Remove a mistaken repo with:

```bash
# only if you meant to throw it away and there are no commits you need
rm -rf .git
```

That deletes Git’s data for that directory, not your files. The first-commit hands-on page builds `desk-api` from scratch so you can see a clean `init`.
